scenes.heading: A skill and a CLI
scenes.narration: narratr turns a document into a narrated video, and it runs entirely on your own machine. It comes in two halves. Claude reads the document and writes the script inside your session. A local command line tool takes it from there and renders the video over the next couple of hours. Nothing is uploaded, and no API bill is generated.

scenes.heading: Six layers
scenes.narration: Six layers do the work. Claude plans the scenes and writes the narration. Chatterbox Turbo speaks it. WhisperX lines the words up against the audio for captions. Remotion draws the slides and animates the diagrams, which come from Mermaid. FFmpeg glues the finished scenes together. Only the first of those runs anywhere other than your laptop.

scenes.heading: Zero dollars a video
scenes.narration: A video costs nothing. Claude runs on the subscription that already powers your session, and everything downstream is local. There is no API credit to buy and no monthly floor to clear. The only real expense is electricity, which comes to under two cents for a full run.

scenes.heading: You pay in hours
scenes.narration: What you pay instead is time. A thirty six minute video takes about two and a half hours of compute, and the great majority of that is narration. The point is that none of it needs you. You start the run and walk away.

scenes.heading: Three decisions
scenes.narration: Three decisions shape everything else. Narration is generated first, and the video timeline is derived from it. The skill stops once it has written the script, because a two and a half hour job does not belong in a conversation. And every stage can resume, because a run that cannot survive a closed laptop lid is a gamble rather than a pipeline.

scenes.heading: The usual failure
scenes.narration: Every document to video project fails the same way. You build the slides first, then try to make the narration fit them. The timing drifts, and there is no way to fix it, because every edit breaks the alignment again.

scenes.heading: Narration is the clock
scenes.narration: So invert it. Narration becomes the master clock. Claude writes the script and splits it into scenes. Text to speech renders each scene and reports exactly how long it turned out to be. Only then does anything get drawn, and the renderer is simply told how much time it has. Synchronisation stops being a problem you solve and becomes one you never have.

scenes.heading: It rescues local voice
scenes.narration: There is a second benefit that was not the point but turned out to matter more. Local speech models drift over long single passages and hold together over short ones. Because the timeline is already cut into scenes, nothing longer than about a minute is ever generated in one go. The structure the clock needed is the same structure the model needed.

scenes.heading: One file divides the work
scenes.narration: One file divides the whole system. Everything before it needs judgment. Everything after it is deterministic compute that never touches a language model again. That file is scenes dot json, and getting the boundary in the right place is most of the design.

scenes.heading: End to end
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["Notion or markdown"] --> B["Claude session"]
    B --> C["scenes.json"]
    C --> D{"Validate"}
    D -- "problems" --> B
    D -- "clean" --> E["Human confirms"]
    E --> F["narratr render"]
    F --> G["video.mp4"]
scenes.narration: Here is the shape of it. A document arrives, from Notion or from a file on disk. Claude turns it into scenes dot json. That gets validated, and if anything is wrong it goes straight back to Claude. When it comes out clean, a human looks at the coverage report and says go. Only then does the renderer start, and it runs on its own until a finished video appears.

scenes.heading: Claude launches and leaves
scenes.narration: Claude does not run the pipeline. It starts a detached process, reports a run identifier, and stops. Streaming forty scenes of progress into a conversation would burn a great deal of context to say something a single status command answers in one line. The source can be anything Claude can read, which is why there is no Notion integration and no need for one.

scenes.heading: Two passes, not one
scenes.narration: The script engine runs in two passes, and the reason is specific. A single instruction to turn a document into a video quietly drops material. Long documents get summarised rather than covered, and nothing tells you it happened. Separating the outline from the prose makes it possible to check coverage mechanically instead of hoping.

scenes.heading: The outline loop
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["Markdown"] --> B["Pass 1: Outline"]
    B --> C["Coverage ledger"]
    C --> D{"All mapped?"}
    D -- "no" --> B
    D -- "yes" --> E["Pass 2: Write scenes"]
    E --> F["scenes.json"]
scenes.narration: The first pass reads the document and maps every block to a scene. That mapping is the coverage ledger. If any block is left unmapped, the pass runs again. Only when everything is accounted for does the second pass write the actual narration, section by section, into the final file.

scenes.heading: The ledger is the cure
scenes.narration: The coverage ledger is what stops material going missing. Every leaf block in the source gets an identifier, and the first pass has to assign each one to a scene. The validator rejects any unmapped block, any mapping that points at a scene which does not exist, and any block that was invented along the way. It runs before a second of compute is spent, and it costs nothing.

scenes.heading: Running inside the session
scenes.narration: An earlier version of this shelled out to a separate Claude process. Running inside the live session instead removed a whole category of problem. There is no subprocess to authenticate, no ambient configuration to pin down so runs stay reproducible, and no exposure to a future change in how that subprocess loads its context. Claude is already the script engine.

scenes.heading: Chatterbox Turbo
scenes.narration: Narration uses Chatterbox Turbo. It is a small model, three hundred and fifty million parameters, under an MIT licence, running on Apple's Metal backend. The numbers that follow were measured on an M4 Pro with twenty four gigabytes of memory, on real runs rather than estimates.

scenes.heading: Turbo is twice as fast
scenes.narration: The measure that matters is the real time factor, meaning seconds of compute per second of audio. The standard model came in between two point nine and three point five. Turbo managed one point five nine, which puts a thirty six minute video at roughly a hundred minutes of narration. Be careful with these figures, though. The variance is wide, and individual scenes have ranged from one and a quarter to over five.

scenes.heading: What Turbo demands
scenes.narration: Turbo comes with conditions. It has no built-in voice at all, so it speaks only as whatever reference clip you hand it, and that clip's quality caps every video you will ever make. The clip and the random seed both need pinning, because consistency across scenes depends on them. Setuptools needs pinning too, for reasons that will become clear. And the weights are nearly four gigabytes, downloaded once.

scenes.heading: Captions come free
scenes.narration: Captions come from forced alignment. WhisperX reads the generated audio and lines the words up against it, producing word level timings locally and for free. It does not care which system produced the audio, which means captions stay independent of every other choice in the stack.

scenes.heading: Three kinds of scene
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["scene + duration"] --> B{"Type?"}
    B -- "diagram" --> C["Mermaid to SVG"]
    B -- "prose" --> D["Slide"]
    B -- "code" --> E["Shiki"]
    C --> F["Tag reveal steps"]
    F --> G["Interpolate"]
    D --> G
    E --> G
    G --> H["scene_N.mp4"]
scenes.narration: The renderer handles three kinds of scene. Diagrams get turned into vector graphics through Mermaid. Prose becomes a slide. Code is syntax highlighted. Whichever path a scene takes, it ends up in the same place, interpolated across the timeline and written out as a short video file of its own.

scenes.heading: Revealing a diagram
scenes.narration: Animating a diagram turns out to be simple. Mermaid emits vector graphics where every node and every edge carries an identifier. Claude groups those identifiers into beats. The renderer interpolates opacity for each group across the scene's duration. That is the whole feature, and it needs no third party service.

scenes.heading: Small renders, then concat
scenes.narration: Scenes render one at a time and get joined afterwards. Remotion slows badly on very long compositions, so forty fifty second renders beat one thirty six minute render. It also means an interrupted run has finished work to keep. The renderer sits behind a written contract, receiving a single scene and its measured duration and nothing else, so it can be replaced without disturbing anything upstream.

scenes.heading: Walk away and come back
scenes.narration: The durability requirement is simple to state. Start a run, walk away, and come back to either a finished video or a run that picks up exactly where it stopped. What you must never come back to is two hours of wasted compute and nothing to show for it.

scenes.heading: How a run resumes
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["Start run"] --> B["Hash doc and config"]
    B --> C{"Manifest?"}
    C -- "no" --> D["Create"]
    C -- "yes" --> E["Load"]
    D --> F["Next pending scene"]
    E --> F
    F --> G["Write then rename"]
    G --> H["Mark done"]
    H --> I{"More?"}
    I -- "yes" --> F
    I -- "no" --> J["Stitch"]
scenes.narration: A run hashes the document and its configuration to get an identifier. If a manifest already exists for that identifier it gets loaded, otherwise a fresh one is created. Then it works through the scenes that are not yet done, writing each to a temporary name and renaming it into place. The manifest is committed after every scene. When none are left, the pieces are stitched together.

scenes.heading: Four rules
scenes.narration: Four rules make that work. Every artefact is keyed on a hash of its own inputs, so a matching file means skip, and resume and incremental re-render fall out of the same mechanism. Writes go to a temporary name and get renamed, so a half written file never looks finished. The manifest is committed after every scene, so the most you lose is about ninety seconds. And the model loads once for the whole run, because loading it costs seventy five seconds.

scenes.heading: Surviving the session
scenes.narration: Detaching is what lets the run outlive the thing that started it. The process forks into its own session group, writes an identifier, and returns in about a second. After that it is independent of the Claude session, the terminal, and the parent shell. Closing any of them changes nothing.

scenes.heading: The remaining gap
scenes.code: caffeinate -is uv run narratr render scenes.json
scenes.narration: Sleep is the one hole left. Wrapping the command in caffeinate keeps the machine from dozing off on its own. But be careful here, because it does not do what most people assume. Closing the lid still puts the machine to sleep unless an external display is attached. So either run it with the lid open on mains power, or lean on the checkpointing and accept losing the scene in flight.

scenes.heading: Mostly build
scenes.narration: Almost everything here is built rather than bought, and the reasoning differs by layer. Nothing off the shelf does coverage guaranteed chunking, so the script engine is custom. The voice model is open source and free to run. The renderer is open source with a timeline already in it. Only the final assembly is genuinely bought, and FFmpeg does that in milliseconds without re-encoding anything.

scenes.heading: What was ruled out
scenes.narration: Two things were evaluated and rejected. Commercial speech services were dropped after a real listening test, because the recurring cost bought nothing that could not be replaced locally. The Anthropic Messages API was dropped too. It offers better determinism and explicit cache control, but it needs separately purchased credits for a tool whose calls the existing subscription already covers.

scenes.heading: Where the hours go
scenes.narration: Here is where the two and a half hours actually go. Narration takes about a hundred minutes. Rendering is somewhere between thirty and sixty. Alignment adds roughly ten, and stitching is instant. Only the narration figure has been measured. The rest are estimates and should be treated as such. Drafting is much cheaper than this, because editing one scene re-renders only that scene.

scenes.heading: What could still go wrong
scenes.narration: Several things could still go wrong. Script quality decides whether the result is worth watching, and that is settled entirely in the prompts. The renderer needs a paid company licence above three people, counted by headcount, with internal use included. Whether the voice holds together across forty scenes has never been tested. And the speed measurements on Apple's backend are erratic in a way that hardware alone does not explain.

scenes.heading: Where it stands
scenes.narration: As things stand, narration works and has been benchmarked. Runs resume correctly and survive the session that started them. The schema and the coverage gate are in place and tested. Alignment, rendering and stitching do not exist yet. They raise an error rather than quietly doing nothing, so a run stops visibly at the edge of what works and leaves the finished audio behind.

scenes.heading: What happens next
scenes.narration: The order of work from here is deliberate. First, record a proper reference clip, because everything inherits it. Then run twenty scenes of a real document and listen straight through, which is the cheapest test of the one risk that could still sink the voice choice. Then alignment, which is the smallest piece left. And benchmark the renderer before writing any scene components, because both the speed question and the licence question get more expensive to answer with every component written.

scenes.heading: Where this came from
scenes.narration: A note on sources. The speed figures were measured on this machine rather than taken from anyone's blog post. The licence terms were read from the vendor's own documentation rather than recalled. Everything else is cited in the plan, so any claim here can be traced back and checked.
